Power made deep in the mountains of Sichuan reaches Jiangsu, 2,000 km away, in just 7 milliseconds.
The electricity in our homes swings back and forth as it flows. It's called alternating current, AC.
Sent that far as it is, a lot of it would simply be lost on the way.
So first it goes through a converter station and becomes direct current, DC, flowing one way only.
Then it races along this line, more than 2,000 km long, all the way to Jiangsu.
The whole trip takes 7 milliseconds, less than the blink of an eye.
At the end it's turned back into AC, stepped down level by level, and sent to the socket in your wall.
Plug in your phone charger, and inside it a tiny part called a bridge rectifier turns the AC back into DC.
Believe it or not, it works on the same circuit principle as the giant, storeys tall, in the converter station.
Only the station's power is a full 400 million times that of this little charger.
Every bar of charge on your phone came this far, across mountains and rivers.
